  Theorem 3.8 and (67) establish the existence of the limits in the skewed case but do not identify
their values.
  The discrepancy between continuous and discrete persistence arises at the boundary: a sampled
path may cross below zero and return above zero between successive observations. For a jump
process, controlling such rescued sub-mesh crossings requires joint control of three quantities:
the mass near zero under the conditioned law, the depth of the first overshoot below zero, and
the probability of returning above zero during the remainder of the mesh interval. An estimate
conditioned on a fixed overshoot depth is insufficient because the first overshoot can be arbitrarily
small. Figure 3 shows the configuration.

Remark 6.3 (Remaining obstacle). If the first downcrossing occurs at time s with overshoot depth z,
the return probability during the remaining interval is

The same three quantities govern Conjecture 6.2, with 1 − ρ in place of 1/2, and the two extremes
of Figure 1(b) degenerate in opposite ways: for 1 < α < 2 and β = 1 there are no negative jumps,
first passage below zero occurs by creeping, and the overshoot vanishes identically, whereas for
β = −1 there are no positive jumps, the overshoot is genuine, and a rescue must be achieved by a
continuous climb. Neither degeneration by itself settles the corresponding dense-sampling limit.△
